title: Quality Improvement
description: Class 14 practice: why quality must improve, federal, state, and local initiatives, nurse-sensitive indicators, the QI process, chart audits, and risk management, incident reports, and quality management programs such as PDSA and root cause analysis.

pressure.intro: A nurse on a 30-bed medical-surgical unit joins the unit's quality improvement team after the unit's rate of hospital-acquired pressure injuries rose for two quarters in a row.

tabs.title: Unit Data
tabs.html:
Unit Data

MeasureQ1Q2Q3
Hospital-acquired pressure injuries per 1,000 client days (national average for similar units: 0.9)1.11.62.4
Stage 3 pressure injuries012
Skin assessment documented within 8 hours of admission70%66%64%
Repositioning documented every 2 hours, day shift84%82%81%
Repositioning documented every 2 hours, night shift71%63%58%

Every client has a pressure-injury risk score on admission. 95% of staff completed skin-care training this year.

tabs.title: Staff Comments
tabs.html:
Staff Comments

  • Night shift: “It's two of us for 15 clients, and the repositioning log is on paper at the desk.”
  • Day shift: “A pressure-relieving mattress takes a day to arrive. We have 6 for 30 beds, and they're usually all in use.”
  • Charge nurse: “Wound care nurse consults take about 3 days.”

tabs.title: Draft Action Plan
tabs.html:
Draft Action Plan

Goal: Lower the rate to 1.0 per 1,000 client days within 6 months.

Change to test: Hourly rounding with repositioning prompts in the electronic record, and the repositioning log moved to the bedside.

Responsible: The unit's QI nurse leads the test; the nurse manager oversees it.

questions.stem: A nurse is explaining what quality health care means. Which of the following definitions from the Institute of Medicine (IOM) should the nurse use?
options: Care that costs the client and the hospital as little as possible, in every case
Care that gives every client whatever services they request, when they request them
The degree to which health services increase the likelihood of desired outcomes and are consistent with current professional knowledge
Care that is provided only by the most experienced staff members on each unit
questions.rationale:
Increasing the likelihood of desired outcomes, consistent with current professional knowledge is correct. That's the IOM's definition of quality: care that makes good outcomes more likely, for individuals and populations, and reflects current knowledge.

The lowest cost isn't the measure of quality; quality management aims for cost-effective care by preventing overuse, misuse, and underuse, not by cutting corners. Whatever clients request may not be appropriate or evidence-based. The most experienced staff doesn't guarantee quality, and every nurse is expected to give quality care.

Takeaway: Quality means better odds of good outcomes, based on current knowledge.

questions.stem: A nurse manager is describing high-quality care to new staff. Which of the following are part of high-quality care?
options: Giving clients the services that are appropriate for them
Providing care in a technically competent way
Choosing the most expensive treatment available
Communicating well with clients and families
Making decisions together with clients
Being sensitive to each client's culture
questions.rationale:
High-quality care means providing clients with appropriate services, in a technically competent manner, with good communication, shared decision making, and cultural sensitivity.

The most expensive treatment isn't automatically the best; unnecessary or costly care can be overuse, which quality management tries to prevent.

Takeaway: Quality care is appropriate, competent, communicative, shared, and culturally sensitive, not necessarily the most expensive.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements defines quality improvement?
options: Systematic, continuous actions that lead to measurable improvements in health care services and in the health of targeted client groups
A one-time inspection of a unit to find staff members who aren't following policy
A research study that tests a new treatment and requires review board approval
A yearly survey that asks clients whether they liked their hospital room
questions.rationale:
Systematic, continuous actions that lead to measurable improvements is correct. This definition, from the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), highlights what makes QI work: it's ongoing, it's organized, and its results are measured.

A one-time inspection to find staff at fault isn't continuous and focuses on blame instead of systems. A research study generates new knowledge, while QI improves local processes using local data. A yearly room survey may collect some data, but on its own it isn't a systematic improvement process.

Takeaway: QI is continuous, systematic, and measurable.

questions.stem: Quality management aims to prevent the overuse, misuse, and underuse of health care. For each example, specify the problem it shows.
rows: A client receives antibiotics for a cold caused by a virus
A client receives the wrong dose of the right medication
An eligible older adult is never offered a pneumococcal vaccine
A client has a repeat CT scan although a recent one is available
A client who has diabetes doesn't get an annual eye exam
A client develops a preventable infection after a properly chosen surgery
questions.rationale:
Overuse is care that isn't needed: antibiotics for a viral cold, and a repeat scan when a recent one exists. Misuse is the right care done wrong, including preventable complications: the wrong dose of the right medication, and a preventable infection after an appropriate surgery. Underuse is needed care that isn't given: a missed vaccine, and a missed eye exam for a client who has diabetes.

Takeaway: Overuse is too much care, misuse is care done wrong, and underuse is care left out; quality management targets all three.

questions.stem: A nurse is explaining how the Institute of Medicine's report To Err Is Human changed the way hospitals respond to errors. Which of the following statements reflects the report's main message?
options: Most errors are caused by careless individuals, who should be removed.
Errors are rare, so tracking them isn't worth the cost.
Only physicians make errors that harm clients.
Most errors come from faulty systems and processes, so the fix is to redesign the systems.
questions.rationale:
Most errors come from faulty systems, so the fix is to redesign them is correct. To Err Is Human (2000) estimated that errors caused about 98,000 hospital deaths a year, and its central message was that good people working in bad systems make mistakes, so safety depends on better systems.

Blaming careless individuals is the approach the report moved away from. Errors are common, not rare. And errors involve every discipline, not only physicians.

Takeaway: Fix the system, not the blame.

questions.stem: Complete the following sentences about the need for quality improvement.
questions.text: The IOM's 2000 report estimated that errors caused about {{0}} deaths a year in U.S. hospitals. A 2011 update estimated {{1}} preventable deaths a year, which would make medical errors the {{2}}.

options: 9.8 million
2.1 to 4 million
about 9,800
third leading cause of death
tenth leading cause of death
rarest cause of death in hospitals
leading cause of death in children

questions.rationale:
To Err Is Human (IOM, 2000) estimated about 98,000 deaths a year in hospitals from errors. An updated study in 2011 estimated 210,000 to 400,000 preventable deaths a year, which would make medical errors the third leading cause of death in the United States.

Takeaway: Hundreds of thousands of preventable deaths are why quality improvement is every nurse's job.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements describes a conclusion of the Institute of Medicine's report Crossing the Quality Chasm?
options: The U.S. health care system was working well and needed only small adjustments to its funding.
The health care system was too disorganized to care well for people with several chronic illnesses, and needed redesign around six aims.
Hospitals should stop measuring quality, because collecting data distracts staff from client care.
Quality would improve on its own if hospitals simply hired more physicians and specialists.
questions.rationale:
The system was too disorganized for people with several chronic illnesses and needed redesign around six aims is correct. Crossing the Quality Chasm (IOM, 2001) proposed six aims for improvement: care that is safe, timely, effective, efficient, equitable, and patient-centered.

The report called for major redesign, not small adjustments. It called for more measurement, not less. And it found the problem was how care is organized, not simply the number of physicians.

Takeaway: The six aims (STEEEP) define quality care: safe, timely, effective, efficient, equitable, and patient-centered.

questions.stem: A clinic prescribes an antibiotic for nearly every sore throat without testing, although evidence shows that most sore throats are caused by viruses. Which of the six aims for improvement is the clinic failing to meet?
options: Effective
Timely
Equitable
Patient-centered
questions.rationale:
Effective is correct. Effective care means providing services based on scientific evidence to everyone who could benefit, and not providing services that are unlikely to help. Antibiotics don't help viral infections, so giving them without testing is ineffective care, and overuse.

Timely is about avoiding harmful delays, equitable is about care that doesn't vary by personal characteristics such as income or race, and patient-centered is about respecting clients' preferences, needs, and values. None of these is the main problem here.

Takeaway: Effective care follows the evidence: give what helps, and skip what doesn't.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked why the hospital invests so much in quality improvement. Which of the following explanations is most accurate?
options: It mainly helps the hospital look good in its advertisements.
It replaces the need for nurses to use clinical judgment.
Measuring care against standards and fixing processes reduces errors, infections, falls, and readmissions.
It's required only once, when the hospital first opens.
questions.rationale:
Measuring care and fixing processes reduces errors, infections, falls, and readmissions is correct. QI connects directly to client outcomes: fewer complications and readmissions, safer care, lower costs, and more satisfied clients.

Good results may help a hospital's reputation, but advertising isn't the purpose. QI supports nurses' judgment rather than replacing it. And QI is continuous, not a one-time requirement.

Takeaway: QI matters because it makes measurable differences in client outcomes.

questions.stem: A nurse notices that, three times this month, clients' 0900 medications weren't given until after 1100 because the pharmacy delivered them late. Which of the following actions best reflects quality improvement?
options: Working faster on mornings when medications arrive late
Asking the pharmacist on duty to apologize to the clients
Telling the clients that late medications are normal on the unit
Reporting the pattern so the team can look at the delivery process and fix it
questions.rationale:
Reporting the pattern so the process can be fixed is correct. A repeated problem points to a system or process issue. QI finds and fixes the process, so every client benefits, not just today's.

Working faster may help one morning but leaves the cause in place. An apology doesn't change the process. Telling clients late medications are normal accepts poor-quality care.

Takeaway: When a problem repeats, report it so the process can be fixed.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements describes the main purpose of quality management?
options: Ranking nurses by how quickly they finish their tasks
Evaluating care processes against accepted standards to correct problems before they harm clients
Replacing the need for accreditation surveys
Finding staff members to discipline after errors
questions.rationale:
Evaluating care against standards to correct problems before they harm clients is correct. Quality management evaluates medical and nursing processes for quality and effectiveness, compared with accepted standards, to correct problems, prevent errors, and provide cost-effective care by preventing overuse, misuse, and underuse.

Speed rankings don't measure quality. Quality management doesn't replace accreditation; it helps organizations meet accreditation standards. Disciplining staff focuses on blame instead of systems.

Takeaway: Quality management compares care with standards to fix problems before clients are harmed.

questions.stem: A unit's QI team wants to know whether the quality of its nursing care is improving. Which of the following data would show this best?
options: The unit's rates of falls and pressure injuries over the past year
The number of nurses hired over the past year
The total hours of overtime worked on the unit
The number of supplies the unit ordered
questions.rationale:
Rates of falls and pressure injuries over time is correct. QI depends on measurable outcomes, and falls and pressure injuries are nurse-sensitive outcomes that reflect the quality of nursing care. Tracking them over time shows whether care is improving.

Hiring, overtime, and supply orders describe staffing and costs. They may affect quality, but they don't measure client outcomes.

Takeaway: Judge the quality of care by client outcomes over time.

questions.stem: For each activity, specify the organization responsible.
columns: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)
rows: Surveys hospitals on site and decides whether they keep their accreditation
Approves nursing education programs and licenses nurses
Lowers payments to hospitals that have too many readmissions within 30 days
Funds research on patient safety and created the TeamSTEPPS teamwork training
questions.rationale:
The Joint Commission accredits health care organizations through on-site surveys, and sets standards such as the National Patient Safety Goals. The state board of nursing enforces the Nurse Practice Act, licenses and disciplines nurses, and approves nursing programs. CMS ties payment to quality, including penalties for too many readmissions. AHRQ funds research on quality and patient safety and created TeamSTEPPS.

Takeaway: CMS pays for quality, The Joint Commission sets and checks standards, AHRQ researches safety, and the state board of nursing licenses and approves.

questions.stem: A client develops a serious, unexpected reaction to a medication that was approved last year. Which of the following agencies collects reports of adverse events like this one?
options: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
The National Institutes of Health (NIH)
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
questions.rationale:
The FDA is correct. The FDA approves and regulates drugs, medical devices, vaccines, and blood, and it collects reports of serious adverse events through its MedWatch program. Those reports can lead to new warnings or recalls.

OSHA protects workers' safety. The NIH funds and conducts medical research. The CDC tracks diseases and infections and publishes infection-control guidelines.

Takeaway: Problems with drugs and devices are reported to the FDA.

questions.stem: A hospital requires staff to use two client identifiers, such as name and date of birth, before every medication and procedure. Which of the following initiatives most directly drives this requirement?
options: Healthy People 2030
OSHA's workplace safety standards
Medicare Part D drug coverage
The Joint Commission's National Patient Safety Goals
questions.rationale:
The Joint Commission's National Patient Safety Goals is correct. These goals target known safety problems, such as identifying clients correctly, and accredited organizations must meet them. Using two identifiers is a long-standing goal.

Healthy People 2030 sets national health objectives for the population. OSHA protects workers. Medicare Part D pays for prescription drugs.

Takeaway: National Patient Safety Goals come from The Joint Commission, and identifying clients correctly is one of them.

questions.stem: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) won't pay hospitals extra for certain conditions that clients acquire during a hospital stay. Which of the following are examples of these conditions?
options: A catheter-associated urinary tract infection
Pneumonia that was present when the client was admitted
A stage 3 pressure injury that developed in the hospital
The planned surgery the client was admitted for
A fall with an injury during the hospital stay
questions.rationale:
CMS ties payment to quality. It won't pay extra for preventable hospital-acquired conditions, such as catheter-associated urinary tract infections, stage 3 and 4 pressure injuries, and falls with injury. It also penalizes hospitals with too many readmissions.

Pneumonia present on admission wasn't acquired in the hospital, and the planned surgery is the reason for the stay, not a complication.

Takeaway: When payment depends on preventing harm, hospitals invest in preventing it.

questions.stem: For each initiative to improve health care, specify whether it is federal, state, or local.
rows: Medicare lowers payments to hospitals with too many readmissions
A city health department offers free blood pressure checks in barbershops
A state law requires hospitals to report certain infections to the state health department
The FDA approves a new vaccine after reviewing safety data
The state board of nursing requires continuing education to renew a nursing license
A county health department inspects restaurants and posts the results
questions.rationale:
Federal initiatives come from national agencies and programs, such as Medicare's readmission penalties and FDA vaccine approval. State initiatives come from state laws and state agencies, such as infection-reporting laws and the board of nursing's license renewal rules. Local initiatives come from city and county health departments, such as community blood pressure checks and restaurant inspections.

Takeaway: Quality and safety are shaped at every level: federal, state, and local.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements explains how accreditation by The Joint Commission drives quality improvement in hospitals?
options: The Joint Commission manages each hospital's daily staffing.
Hospitals must meet evidence-based standards and show continuous improvement to keep their accreditation.
The Joint Commission licenses each nurse who works in an accredited hospital.
The Joint Commission pays for every hospital's QI projects.
questions.rationale:
Meeting evidence-based standards and showing continuous improvement is correct. To be reaccredited, an organization must show that it continuously evaluates its performance, corrects deficiencies, and improves, and on-site surveys check this. That makes QI an ongoing requirement.

The Joint Commission doesn't manage daily staffing, license nurses (the state board of nursing does), or pay for QI projects.

Takeaway: Accreditation keeps QI going, because hospitals must keep proving that they meet standards and improve.

questions.stem: After several nurses are assaulted in the emergency department, the hospital adds panic buttons and violence-prevention training. Which of the following statements about OSHA's role is accurate?
options: OSHA sets standards that protect the health and safety of workers, including nurses.
OSHA approves new medications before they can be given to clients.
OSHA tracks infectious disease outbreaks across the country.
OSHA accredits hospitals and publishes National Patient Safety Goals.
questions.rationale:
OSHA protects workers' health and safety is correct. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration requires employers to provide a safe workplace and reduce hazards, including workplace violence, needlesticks, and chemical exposures. It protects staff, not clients.

Approving medications is the FDA's role. Tracking outbreaks is the CDC's. Accrediting hospitals and setting patient safety goals is The Joint Commission's.

Takeaway: OSHA is about the occupational safety of workers.

questions.stem: A hospital reports its rates of central line infections to a national CDC system that lets it compare its rates with other hospitals' rates. Which of the following is the main purpose of this reporting?
options: To decide which nurses caused each infection
To replace the hospital's own infection-control program
To set the price that insurers pay for central lines
To track and compare health care-associated infections so hospitals can find and fix problems
questions.rationale:
Tracking and comparing infections so hospitals can find and fix problems is correct. The CDC tracks health care-associated infections through its national reporting system and publishes infection-control guidelines. Comparing a hospital's rates with others' shows where it needs to improve.

The goal is system improvement, not finding who caused each infection. National data support the hospital's own program rather than replacing it, and they don't set prices.

Takeaway: National infection data let hospitals compare themselves with others and focus their improvement work.

questions.stem: A nurse tells the nurse manager about a near miss: the nurse almost gave a medication to the wrong client but caught it at the bedside. Which of the following responses by the manager best supports quality improvement?
options: Writing the nurse up so the mistake isn't repeated
Thanking the nurse for reporting, and reviewing the process that allowed the near miss
Telling the nurse that near misses don't need to be reported, since no harm occurred
Posting the nurse's name at the nurses' station as a reminder to others
questions.rationale:
Thanking the nurse and reviewing the process is correct. Near misses show weaknesses in a system before anyone is harmed, so QI depends on staff reporting them. Responding without blame keeps people reporting, and looking at the process finds the real fix.

Writing the nurse up and posting their name punish reporting, so future near misses go unreported. Not reporting near misses throws away the chance to fix a problem before it harms someone.

Takeaway: Reward reporting and fix the process; near misses are free lessons.

questions.stem: Which of the following actions reflect a staff nurse's role in quality improvement?
options: Reporting errors, near misses, and unsafe conditions
Leaving quality improvement to the nurse managers
Collecting data for unit audits, such as fall tracking
Joining the unit's QI team or practice council
Not mentioning coworkers' mistakes, to protect them
Following protocols consistently so results can be measured
questions.rationale:
Staff nurses are central to QI: they identify and report problems (errors, near misses, unsafe conditions), collect data, join QI teams, councils, and root cause analyses, and follow protocols consistently so a change can be measured fairly. Nurses at the bedside are well positioned to spot risks.

Leaving QI to managers wastes the bedside view. Hiding coworkers' mistakes lets the same system problems keep harming clients.

Takeaway: Every nurse does QI: speak up, report, collect data, and take part.

questions.stem: Complete the following sentence about how quality improvement relates to other concepts.
questions.text: Quality improvement relates to {{0}}, because its main goal is preventing errors and harm, and to {{1}}, because data from electronic records are used to compare a unit's results with others'.

options: health policy
safety
culture
growth and development
informatics
ethics
spirituality
nutrition

questions.rationale:
QI relates to safety, because preventing errors and harm is its central goal, and to informatics, because electronic data collection, comparison with other units, and decision support make measurement possible.

QI also connects to health policy (CMS payment rules and accreditation standards drive QI), evidence-based practice, accountability, and communication, but those don't fit the reasons given in the sentence.

Takeaway: QI is tied to safety (its goal) and informatics (its data).

questions.stem: A QI team wants to know whether clients feel respected and included in decisions about their care. Which of the following data sources should the team use?
options: Client satisfaction and experience surveys
Incident reports filed on the unit
The unit's staffing schedules
Invoices for the unit's supplies
questions.rationale:
Client satisfaction and experience surveys is correct. Clients' own reports are the best data about whether care feels respectful and shared, which are parts of quality, patient-centered care. Nurses are well positioned to analyze client satisfaction and act on it.

Incident reports capture events that harmed or could harm someone, not clients' sense of respect. Staffing schedules and supply invoices describe resources, not clients' experience.

Takeaway: To measure patient-centered care, ask the clients.

questions.stem: A nurse notices that the unit's new bed alarms are easy to switch off by accident when clients reposition. Which of the following actions best reflects the nurse's role in quality improvement?
options: Taping over the switch on the nurse's own clients' beds, without telling anyone
Waiting to see whether a client falls before saying anything
Reporting the problem through the proper channels and suggesting a fix to the QI team
Turning off the alarms, since they don't work reliably
questions.rationale:
Reporting the problem and suggesting a fix is correct. The bedside nurse is well positioned to spot equipment and process risks, and reporting them lets the organization fix the problem for every client, which is proactive risk management.

A private workaround leaves other units at risk and may create new hazards. Waiting for a fall turns a preventable risk into harm. Turning off the alarms removes a safety measure.

Takeaway: Report risks before they cause harm, so the system gets fixed.

questions.stem: Which of the following QSEN competencies asks nurses to use data to monitor the outcomes of care and to test changes that improve them?
options: Informatics
Teamwork and collaboration
Patient-centered care
Quality improvement
questions.rationale:
Quality improvement is correct. QSEN's quality improvement competency asks nurses to use data to monitor outcomes and to use improvement methods to design and test changes.

Informatics is about using information and technology. Teamwork and collaboration is about working effectively with others. Patient-centered care is about recognizing the client as a full partner. All six QSEN competencies work together, but this description is quality improvement.

Takeaway: QSEN's QI competency: measure outcomes, test changes, and improve.

questions.stem: A QI team is choosing a change to reduce catheter-associated infections on its unit. Which of the following approaches is best?
options: Choosing whatever change the most senior nurse prefers
Basing the change on the best available evidence, then testing it with the unit's own data
Copying another hospital's change without checking whether it worked
Making several changes at once without measuring any of them
questions.rationale:
Basing the change on the best evidence, then testing it with local data is correct. QI and evidence-based practice work together: the change should be built on the best evidence, and the unit's own data show whether it works there.

The senior nurse's preference is tradition, not evidence. Copying without checking results skips both evidence and measurement. Several unmeasured changes make it impossible to tell what helped.

Takeaway: Choose changes from the evidence, and prove them with your own data.

questions.stem: A unit's QI team is working through the quality improvement process. Place the steps in order.
items: Analyze the unit's current protocols and outcomes
Compare the results with those of leaders in high-quality care
Research the factors that lead to better outcomes
Put changes in place to improve outcomes
Analyze outcomes to see whether the changes worked
questions.rationale:
The QI process is continuous and has several steps: analyze current protocols and outcomes, compare them with leaders in high-quality care (benchmarking), identify areas for improvement, research what leads to better outcomes, implement changes, and analyze the outcomes to see whether the changes worked and find further improvements. A facility that improves should share its methods so others can improve too.

Takeaway: Measure, compare, target, research, change, and measure again.

questions.stem: A client dies after a medication error in an accredited hospital. Which of the following statements describes The Joint Commission's role after this sentinel event?
options: It reviews how the hospital responded, including its root cause analysis and action plan, as part of accreditation.
It decides whether the nurse involved keeps their license.
It takes over the hospital's operations until the investigation ends.
It has no role, because each hospital handles its own errors privately.
questions.rationale:
It reviews the hospital's response, including the root cause analysis and action plan is correct. A sentinel event, an unexpected occurrence involving death, serious physical or psychological injury, or the risk of it, requires immediate investigation and response. The Joint Commission expects a thorough root cause analysis and a plan to reduce future risk, and it reviews the response as part of accreditation.

Licensure decisions belong to the state board of nursing. The Joint Commission doesn't take over hospitals. And sentinel events aren't handled privately: accreditors expect a documented response.

Takeaway: After a sentinel event come a root cause analysis, an action plan, and The Joint Commission's review.

questions.stem: Which of the following situations is a breach of care?
options: A nurse reports a near miss to the charge nurse.
A client who has been told the risks declines a bath.
A nurse doesn't reassess a client's pain after giving an opioid, although the policy requires it.
A nurse asks for help programming an unfamiliar infusion pump.
questions.rationale:
Not reassessing after an opioid, as the policy requires is correct. A breach of care occurs when a nurse does something that shouldn't have been done, or doesn't do something that should have been done. Missing a required reassessment is an omission, and nurses are most often involved in breaches around bedside assessment and monitoring.

Reporting a near miss and asking for help with unfamiliar equipment are safe, expected practices. A client's informed refusal is the client's right, not a breach, as long as it's respected and documented.

Takeaway: A breach of care is doing what shouldn't be done, or not doing what should be.

questions.stem: Which of the following actions help a nurse reduce the risk of a breach of care?
options: Reporting problems to supervisors
Skipping documentation on busy shifts
Staying current in skills and education
Basing care on a nursing model, and documenting the care and the client's response
Avoiding questions so they look competent
questions.rationale:
Nurses reduce the risk of a breach of care by reporting problems to supervisors, staying current in skills and education, and basing all care on a nursing model and documenting the care and the client's response.

Skipping documentation leaves no proof that care was given. Avoiding questions leads to mistakes with unfamiliar tasks; asking is safe practice.

Takeaway: Speak up, stay current, and document care and responses.

questions.stem: After a client falls, the risk manager reviews what happened, makes sure the client's injury is treated, and works to prevent another fall. Which part of risk management does this describe?
options: Proactive risk management
Benchmarking
Accreditation
Reactive risk management
questions.rationale:
Reactive risk management is correct. Risk management has proactive parts, which prevent adverse events, and reactive parts, which minimize the damage after an event happens, and it must happen every day. Responding to a fall that already occurred is reactive.

Proactive risk management would identify and reduce fall risks before anyone falls. Benchmarking compares outcomes with leaders. Accreditation is an external review of an organization against standards.

Takeaway: Before an event: proactive. After an event: reactive.

questions.stem: Which of the following activities are part of a hospital's risk management process?
options: Identifying risks that could lead to client or staff injury or financial loss
Reviewing the systems that monitor those risks
Analyzing how often past adverse events happened, how severe they were, and why
Keeping up to date on health care laws
Assigning blame for each adverse event to one staff member
Identifying the need for client and staff education
questions.rationale:
The risk management process identifies risks of client or staff injury or financial loss, reviews the systems that monitor risks, analyzes the frequency, severity, and causes of past adverse events, stays current on health care laws, and identifies education needs.

Assigning blame to one person isn't part of it: like root cause analysis, risk management looks at systems, so the same event doesn't happen again.

Takeaway: Risk management finds, monitors, analyzes, and teaches; it doesn't hunt for someone to blame.

questions.stem: A nurse completes an incident report after giving a client the wrong dose of a medication. Which of the following statements about the report is accurate?
options: It is placed in the client's medical record.
It is sent to risk management or the quality department per policy, and it isn't part of the medical record.
It is given to the client's family so they know what happened.
The nurse keeps a copy at home in case of a lawsuit.
questions.rationale:
It goes to risk management or the quality department, not into the medical record is correct. An incident (occurrence) report documents any event out of the ordinary that harmed or could have harmed a client, employee, or visitor. It's a confidential QI and risk management tool, used to find patterns and fix systems, and access is limited to risk management, QI staff, and administrators.

It's never placed in the client's record, and the record shouldn't mention it. It isn't given to the family; the client and family are told what happened through the facility's disclosure process. Copies taken home break confidentiality.

Takeaway: Chart the facts of the event in the record; send the incident report to risk management, never into the chart.

questions.stem: A nurse finds a client on the floor beside the bed. Place the nurse's actions in order.
items: Assess the client for injury and give the care needed
Notify the provider and the charge nurse
Document the facts of the event and the care given in the client's record
questions.rationale:
The client comes first: assess for injury and give the care needed. Then notify the provider and the charge nurse. Next, document the facts in the client's record: what the nurse observed, the care given, and who was notified. Finally, complete the incident report for risk management.

Takeaway: Assess and treat, notify, document the facts, then file the incident report.

questions.stem: Which of the following belong in an incident report about a client's fall?
options: The date, time, and place of the event
The nurse's opinion about who was at fault
What the nurse saw, described objectively
The care given and who was notified
A note that a copy will be placed in the client's chart
questions.rationale:
An incident report gives objective facts: the date, time, and place, what the nurse saw and the client's condition, and the care given and who was notified. It's completed by the nurse who witnessed or discovered the event, as soon as possible.

Opinions about fault don't belong, because the report is for finding system problems, not blame. And incident reports are never placed in the chart.

Takeaway: Incident reports are factual, prompt, blame-free, and kept out of the chart.

questions.stem: A hospital's QI team wants to reduce medication errors. Which of the following strategies should the team use?
options: Bar-code scanning of client ID bands and medications
Taking verbal orders for routine medications to save time
Computerized provider order entry
A pharmacist's review before the first dose of a new medication
Storing look-alike medications next to each other
Labels that highlight the differences between look-alike, sound-alike drug names
questions.rationale:
Strategies that reduce medication errors include bar-code scanning, computerized provider order entry, a pharmacy first-dose review, and managing look-alike, sound-alike names, for example with labels that highlight the differences (such as “hydrOXYzine” and “hydrALAZINE”) and storing those drugs apart.

Verbal orders for routine medications add risk; they're for urgent situations only. Storing look-alikes together invites mix-ups.

Takeaway: Medication safety comes from layered checks: scanning, electronic orders, pharmacy review, and clear labels.

questions.stem: A client develops a rash and wheezing after receiving a prescribed antibiotic. Which of the following terms describes harm that a client experiences from exposure to a medication?
options: An adverse drug event
A near miss
Medication reconciliation
A breach of confidentiality
questions.rationale:
An adverse drug event is correct. It's harm a client experiences as a result of exposure to a medication, whether from an allergic reaction, an error, or a known risk of the drug. Many adverse drug events are preventable.

A near miss is an error caught before it reaches the client, so there's no harm. Medication reconciliation is comparing a client's medication lists to prevent errors. A breach of confidentiality is about privacy.

Takeaway: Harm from a medication is an adverse drug event, and many of them are preventable.

questions.stem: A unit is using the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle to improve hand hygiene. Which 2 activities belong in the Study phase?
options: Setting a goal of 90% hand-hygiene compliance in 3 months
Comparing the hand-hygiene rate during the trial with the baseline rate
Placing hand sanitizer at every doorway on one unit for 4 weeks
Analyzing whether the trial unit's infection rate changed
Adding sanitizer at every doorway in the hospital after the trial succeeds
Deciding who will collect the audit data, and how
questions.rationale:
In the Study phase, the team analyzes the data and compares the results with its predictions and the baseline: comparing compliance with the baseline and analyzing whether infections changed.

Setting a goal and deciding who collects data belong in Plan. Placing sanitizer on one unit for 4 weeks is Do, a small-scale test. Spreading the change hospital-wide is Act.

Takeaway: Plan it, Do it small, Study the data, and Act on the results.

questions.stem: A QI team has planned a new handoff tool to reduce communication errors. Which of the following actions represents the Do phase of the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle?
options: Using the tool on every unit in the hospital starting next week
Comparing the error rates before and after the tool was used
Using the tool on one unit for 2 weeks and recording any problems
Making the tool part of hospital policy
questions.rationale:
Using the tool on one unit for 2 weeks and recording problems is correct. The Do phase carries out the change on a small scale, as a pilot test, while collecting data and noting problems.

Using it hospital-wide right away is the common trap: spreading the change comes in Act, after Study shows it works. Comparing error rates is Study. Making it policy is Act.

Takeaway: “Do” means a small test first, never the full rollout.

questions.stem: For each description, specify the quality management approach.
rows: After a client's unexpected death, a team finds the underlying system causes
Uses statistics to cut variation and defects, following Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, and Control
Before a new unit opens, a team predicts how its medication process could fail and fixes the riskiest steps
Removes wasted steps that add no value for the client, such as repeated registration and long waits
questions.rationale:
Root cause analysis is reactive: after an adverse or sentinel event, it finds the underlying system causes. Six Sigma uses statistics to reduce variation and defects through Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, and Control (DMAIC). FMEA is proactive: before harm occurs, it predicts how a process could fail and redesigns it. Lean eliminates waste and steps that add no value, to improve flow.

Takeaway: RCA looks back after harm, FMEA looks ahead before harm, Six Sigma cuts variation, and Lean cuts waste.

questions.stem: A hospital wants every department, from housekeeping to surgery, to take part in improving quality all the time, with a focus on what clients need. Which of the following approaches fits this goal best?
options: A single root cause analysis
A failure mode and effects analysis of one process
A yearly inspection by the nurse manager
Total quality management (continuous quality improvement)
questions.rationale:
Total quality management (continuous quality improvement) is correct. TQM/CQI is an organization-wide philosophy: everyone, at every level, continuously improves processes, with a focus on the client and decisions based on data.

A root cause analysis and an FMEA each examine one event or one process. A yearly inspection isn't continuous and doesn't involve everyone.

Takeaway: TQM/CQI means everyone, everywhere, improving all the time.

questions.stem: A 4-week test of a new medication-pass routine on one unit cut interruptions and errors in half, with no new problems. Which of the following actions belongs in the Act phase?
options: Running the same 4-week test again on the same unit
Adopting the routine, updating the policy, and spreading it to other units
Deciding which data to collect during the test
Ending the routine, since the test is over
questions.rationale:
Adopting the routine, updating the policy, and spreading it is correct. In the Act phase, the team decides to adopt, adapt (modify), or abandon the change. A successful test is adopted and standardized.

Repeating the same test adds nothing when the results were clear. Deciding which data to collect belongs in Plan. Ending a change that worked throws away the improvement.

Takeaway: In Act, adopt, adapt, or abandon the change, based on what Study showed.

questions.stem: Why does the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle repeat instead of ending after one round?
options: Each round's results lead to the next test of change, so improvement keeps going.
The first round always fails, so the team has to try again.
Accreditors require exactly three rounds for every change.
Repeating the cycle lets the team skip measuring results.
questions.rationale:
Each round's results lead to the next test is correct. Quality improvement is continuous: what the team learns in one cycle shapes the next plan, so changes are refined in small steps.

First rounds often succeed, and accreditors don't require a set number of cycles. Every cycle includes measuring results; that's the Study phase.

Takeaway: PDSA is a loop: each cycle teaches something that starts the next one.

questions.stem: During a root cause analysis, a team draws a diagram that groups the possible causes of an error into categories, such as people, methods, equipment, and environment. Which tool is the team using?
options: A run chart
A PICOT question
A fishbone (cause-and-effect) diagram
A pie chart of staffing
questions.rationale:
A fishbone (cause-and-effect) diagram is correct. It sorts possible causes into categories, so a root cause analysis team can see every contributing factor, not just the most obvious one. Asking “why?” repeatedly (the 5 Whys) is another RCA tool.

A run chart shows data over time. A PICOT question frames a clinical question for an evidence search. A pie chart of staffing shows proportions, not causes.

Takeaway: Fishbone diagrams and the 5 Whys help an RCA dig past the obvious to the root cause.

questions.stem: Click to highlight the findings that point to areas the QI team should target.
questions.passage:
[[The pressure-injury rate rose from 1.1 to 2.4 per 1,000 client days, against a national average of 0.9]].
[[Every client has a risk score on admission]].
[[Skin assessments within 8 hours of admission fell to 64%]].
[[Night-shift repositioning documentation fell to 58%]].
[[95% of staff completed skin-care training this year]].
[[Pressure-relieving mattresses take a day to arrive]].
questions.rationale:
The targets are the rising pressure-injury rate, well above the national average, skin assessments within 8 hours falling to 64%, night-shift repositioning falling to 58%, and a day's wait for pressure-relieving mattresses. Each one shows a gap between current care and best practice.

Risk scores on admission and 95% of staff trained are strengths: the problem isn't knowledge or risk screening, but follow-through on assessments, repositioning, and equipment.

Takeaway: QI targets the gaps between current performance and the benchmark, and notes the strengths to build on.

questions.stem: Complete the following sentence about the unit data.
questions.text: Comparing the unit's rate with the national average for similar units is called {{0}}, and because the rate keeps rising, the team's next step is to {{1}}.

options: accreditation
benchmarking
triage
randomization
wait another quarter to be sure
stop documenting repositioning
identify the causes and test a change
transfer high-risk clients to other units

questions.rationale:
Comparing a unit's outcomes with those of leaders or similar units is benchmarking, a step in the QI process. A rising rate well above the benchmark calls for the team to identify the causes and test a change.

Accreditation is an external review against standards, triage sorts clients by urgency, and randomization assigns research participants to groups. Waiting another quarter lets more clients be harmed, stopping documentation hides the problem, and transferring high-risk clients moves the problem instead of fixing it.

Takeaway: Benchmark to see the gap, then find the causes and test a fix.

questions.stem: The team is planning its test of the change. For each potential action, specify whether it is indicated or not indicated.
rows: Test hourly rounding on one hallway for 6 weeks before deciding on more
Start hourly rounding on every unit in the hospital next week
Find out which night nurses missed repositioning and discipline them
Move the repositioning log from the desk to each client's bedside
Track repositioning documentation weekly and the injury rate monthly during the test
Stop measuring once staff say they like the new routine
questions.rationale:
Indicated: testing the change on a small scale first (the Do phase of PDSA), fixing the process problem staff identified (the log kept at the desk), and measuring both the process (repositioning documentation) and the outcome (the injury rate).

Not indicated: a hospital-wide rollout before the test shows results; disciplining night nurses, which blames individuals for a system problem (two nurses for 15 clients, and a log away from the bedside); and stopping measurement based on opinions instead of data.

Takeaway: Test small, fix the process, and keep measuring; don't blame people or spread a change too soon.

questions.stem: The nurse manager reviews the draft action plan. Which of the following elements should a complete action plan include?
options: Who is responsible for carrying out and overseeing the changes
A pilot test of the change
A list of staff members who will be disciplined
Timelines for putting the changes in place
Strategies for measuring whether the changes work
A promise that no client will ever develop a pressure injury
questions.rationale:
A complete action plan identifies who is responsible for implementing and overseeing the improvements, includes pilot testing, sets timelines, and states strategies for measuring effectiveness. The draft has a goal, a change to test, and responsible people, but it still needs a timeline for each step and a measurement plan.

A list of staff to discipline focuses on blame instead of systems, and a promise of zero injuries isn't a measurable plan.

Takeaway: An action plan answers who, pilot, when, and how it will be measured.

questions.stem: After the 6-week test on one hallway, the team compares the results with the unit's Q3 data. For each finding, specify whether it shows improvement, no change, or a decline.
rows: Pressure injuries per 1,000 client days: 2.4 → 1.2
Night-shift repositioning documentation: 58% → 88%
Skin assessments within 8 hours of admission: 64% → 65%
Days to get a wound care consult: 3 → 5
questions.rationale:
The injury rate fell by half, and night-shift repositioning rose to 88%: both improved, so the change is working on the problem it targeted. Admission skin assessments barely moved, so they need their own change in the next cycle. Wound care consults got slower, a decline to report and address.

In the Act phase, the team can adopt hourly rounding more widely and plan the next PDSA cycle for admission skin assessments and consult delays.

Takeaway: Evaluate each measure separately: keep what worked, and plan the next cycle for what didn't change or got worse.

questions.stem: A unit's QI team has chosen falls as the area of care it most needs to improve. Which of the following steps of the quality improvement process should the team take next?
options: Put a new fall-prevention routine in place on the unit
Analyze the outcomes to see whether the changes worked
Research the factors that lead to fewer falls
Compare the unit's fall rate with the rates at leading hospitals
questions.rationale:
The QI process moves in order: analyze current care and outcomes, compare them with leaders in high-quality care (benchmarking), identify areas for improvement, research the factors that lead to better outcomes, put changes in place, and analyze the outcomes. This team has identified its area (falls), so it next researches what reduces falls, such as the evidence and the methods that leading hospitals use.

Putting a routine in place before the research skips the evidence the change should be built on. Analyzing outcomes comes after a change is in place. Comparing with leading hospitals comes before choosing the area to improve.

Takeaway: Identify the area to improve, then research what works before changing practice.

questions.stem: A unit's QI team has started using a new discharge-teaching checklist to reduce readmissions. Which of the following steps of the quality improvement process should the team take next?
options: Analyze the outcomes to see whether readmissions went down
Spread the checklist to every unit in the hospital
Identify the areas where the unit needs to improve
Research the factors that lead to fewer readmissions
questions.rationale:
In the QI process, putting changes in place is followed by analyzing the outcomes to see whether the changes worked: here, whether readmissions went down. The results then point to areas for further improvement, and the process continues.

Spreading the checklist before checking the results could spread a change that doesn't work. Identifying the areas to improve and researching the factors that lead to fewer readmissions came before the team chose the checklist.

Takeaway: After a change is in place, measure the outcomes to see whether it worked.

questions.stem: A QI team is starting a PDSA cycle to reduce catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs). Which of the following activities belongs in the Plan phase?
options: Using a new catheter-removal checklist on one unit
Comparing infection rates before and after the trial
Adopting the checklist on every unit of the hospital
Setting a goal and deciding how infections will be measured
questions.rationale:
The Plan phase identifies the problem, sets a measurable goal, predicts what will happen, chooses the change to test, and decides how results will be measured and who is responsible.

Using the checklist on one unit is the Do phase (a small test). Comparing rates before and after is the Study phase. Adopting it everywhere is a decision in the Act phase.

Takeaway: Plan: set the goal, choose the change, and decide how to measure the results.

questions.stem: A QI team used the PDSA cycle to test a turning-reminder board for preventing hospital-acquired pressure injuries. Which of the following statements from the team's report represents the Study phase?
options: “The board will be added to every medical-surgical unit next month, and the policy updated.”
“Pressure injuries fell from 8 to 4 during the test, as the team predicted.”
“The team predicts that the board will cut pressure injuries in half within 6 weeks.”
“The board was used on one unit for 6 weeks while staff recorded any problems.”
questions.rationale:
The Study phase analyzes the data from the test and compares the results with the baseline and the prediction: pressure injuries fell from 8 to 4, as the team expected.

Predicting the result belongs to Plan. Using the board on one unit while recording problems is Do, the small-scale test. Adding the board to every unit and updating the policy is Act, after Study shows the change worked.

Takeaway: Study: analyze the results and compare them with the prediction and the baseline.

questions.stem: A small test of a new oral-care routine didn't lower the unit's rate of hospital-acquired pneumonia. Which of the following actions fits the Act phase of the PDSA cycle?
options: Adapting or abandoning the change, then planning another test
Adopting the change on every unit
Stopping all work on preventing pneumonia
Repeating the same test with no changes
questions.rationale:
In the Act phase, the team decides what to do with what it learned: adopt a change that worked, adapt it, or abandon it. A change that didn't work is adapted or abandoned, and the cycle starts again with a new plan.

Adopting a change that didn't help spreads it without benefit. Stopping the work leaves the problem unsolved. Repeating the same test unchanged is unlikely to give a different result.

Takeaway: Act: adopt a change that worked; adapt or abandon one that didn't, and plan the next cycle.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the unit's quality data. Which of the following is a nurse-sensitive quality indicator?
options: The number of surgeries performed each month
The average wait for laboratory results
The number of clients admitted each day
The rate of client falls with injury
questions.rationale:
Nurse-sensitive indicators measure outcomes and processes that nursing care directly affects. Falls with injury is one: rounding, fall-risk assessment, and safety measures by nurses change the rate. The National Database of Nursing Quality Indicators (NDNQI) collects these measures.

The number of surgeries and the number of admissions measure how busy the hospital is, not the quality of nursing care. The wait for laboratory results depends mainly on the laboratory.

Takeaway: Nurse-sensitive indicators, such as falls with injury, reflect outcomes that nursing care affects.

questions.stem: A nurse is learning about the National Database of Nursing Quality Indicators (NDNQI). Which of the following are nurse-sensitive indicators?
options: Rates of hospital-acquired pressure injuries
The number of physicians on the medical staff
Rates of catheter-associated urinary tract infections
Rates of central line-associated bloodstream infections
The number of MRI scans done each month
Nurse staffing and skill mix
questions.rationale:
Nurse-sensitive indicators include pressure injuries, catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs), central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSIs), and falls: outcomes that nursing care, such as turning, catheter care, and line care, directly affects. Staffing and skill mix are structure indicators: how many nurses there are and how they're prepared affects these outcomes.

The number of physicians and the number of MRI scans measure staffing and volume outside nursing, not nursing quality.

Takeaway: NDNQI indicators include falls, pressure injuries, CAUTIs, CLABSIs, and nurse staffing.

questions.stem: A nursing student asks why some quality indicators are called nurse-sensitive. Which of the following responses by the nurse is accurate?
options: “Nurses are the ones who collect the data for them.”
“Only nurses are allowed to see the results.”
“They reflect outcomes that nursing care directly affects.”
“They measure how satisfied nurses are with their jobs.”
questions.rationale:
An indicator is nurse-sensitive when nursing care, or how nursing is staffed, directly affects it, so it shows the quality of nursing care. Comparing these indicators with national benchmarks helps units find where to improve.

Who collects the data or who may see the results doesn't make an indicator nurse-sensitive. Nurses' job satisfaction is tracked too, but it isn't what the term means.

Takeaway: Nurse-sensitive indicators measure what nursing care affects.

questions.stem: A unit's results on a nurse-sensitive indicator are worse than the national benchmark for similar units. Which of the following conclusions should the unit's QI team draw?
options: The clients on the unit are sicker, so no change is needed
The nursing care processes behind the indicator need review
The national data are probably wrong for this unit
The nurses involved in each case should be disciplined
questions.rationale:
A nurse-sensitive indicator that's worse than the benchmark for similar units points to nursing care processes that need improving. The team reviews how the care is done (for example, with a PDSA cycle or a chart audit) and plans changes.

Benchmarks compare similar units, so assuming the clients are sicker or the data are wrong dismisses a real signal. QI looks at systems and processes, not discipline of individuals.

Takeaway: When a nurse-sensitive indicator falls behind the benchmark, review and improve the nursing care processes.

questions.stem: A unit's QI team pulls 20 client records to check whether nurses documented a fall-risk score every shift, as policy requires. Which of the following activities is the team carrying out?
options: A root cause analysis
An incident report
A failure mode and effects analysis
A chart audit
questions.rationale:
A chart audit reviews a sample of records to check whether documentation is complete and meets the standard, such as a fall-risk score every shift. The results show how well a practice is being followed.

A root cause analysis looks for the system causes of one serious event. An incident report describes a specific event, such as a fall. A failure mode and effects analysis predicts how a process could fail before harm happens.

Takeaway: A chart audit checks records for complete, correct documentation.

questions.stem: A QI team reviews 25 client records and finds that a skin assessment was documented every shift in only 15 of them. Which of the following actions should the team take next?
options: Ask the nurses to add the missing assessments to those records now
Stop reviewing records, since most of them were complete
Share the results, plan a change, and review the records again later
Discipline each nurse whose record was missing an assessment
questions.rationale:
Audit results are used to improve the process: the team shares the results with staff, plans a change (such as education or a reminder in the electronic record), and audits again later to see whether documentation improves.

Filling in assessments now for past shifts would make the records inaccurate, since no one can see the skin as it was then. Stopping ignores a 40% gap. QI focuses on processes, not discipline of individuals.

Takeaway: Use audit results to change the process, then audit again to measure the improvement.

questions.stem: A client received 10 times the prescribed dose of insulin and was transferred to intensive care. Which of the following questions should the team ask during the root cause analysis?
options: Were two strengths of insulin stored next to each other?
Was the nurse interrupted while preparing the dose?
Which nurse made the error, so that nurse can be disciplined?
Was a second nurse available to double-check the dose?
What kind of health insurance does the client have?
questions.rationale:
A root cause analysis looks at the systems and processes that allowed the error: how the medications were stored, interruptions during preparation, and whether a double-check was available. The answers lead to an action plan that makes the error less likely to happen again.

Finding someone to discipline isn't the goal: an RCA focuses on systems, not individual blame, so staff can report errors openly. The client's insurance has nothing to do with how the error happened.

Takeaway: A root cause analysis asks how systems and processes allowed the error, not who to blame.

questions.stem: During a root cause analysis, the team keeps asking why each cause happened until it reaches a problem in the system. Which of the following techniques is the team using?
options: The 5 Whys
A chart audit
A PDSA cycle
A fishbone diagram
questions.rationale:
The 5 Whys technique asks “why?” again and again, about five times, moving past the first answer to the underlying system cause.

A fishbone diagram is another root cause analysis tool, which sorts possible causes into categories rather than following one chain of whys. A chart audit checks documentation, and a PDSA cycle tests a change.

Takeaway: The 5 Whys follows one cause back, why by why, to the system problem.
